title: Go to the ant
hook: go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways (Proverbs 6:6)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bezalel, filled with the spirit to work in gold, stone and wood. Your line was craft is holy. What did your hands make? Day eight hundred eighty-four.

A line of ants crosses a kitchen counter, each one hauling a crumb bigger than its head. One response is a sponge. The book of Proverbs has another: “Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.” Not a king, not a sage, not a prophet. The teacher, for once, is tiny, and the student is someone who can't get out of bed. Today: go to the ant.
screen: `A LINE OF ANTS ON THE COUNTER.` → `CONSIDER HER WAYS.` → `A VERY SMALL TEACHER.`

segments.voice: First, meet the sluggard. Proverbs has fun with him. He won't go out, he says, because there's a lion in the street. And then this: “As the door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed.” Turning and turning, going nowhere. It's a laugh line, and the laugh is aimed at a habit, not at a person. Second, no boss. The ant, Proverbs says, works “having no guide, overseer, or ruler.” Nobody stands over her with a clipboard. The work starts from inside. That's the lesson aimed at the sluggard: not more supervision, but his own reason to get up. Third, timing. The ant “provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest.” She works while the work can be done, so that later there's enough. Some work can't be crammed into the night before. Fourth, small and wise. Later in Proverbs the ants come back, in a list of creatures “little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise.” They are “a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer.” Wisdom here isn't size or strength. It's steady effort, at the right time, with nobody watching. The ant has a neighbor's echo, too: in the Qur'an, a surah is named for the ant, an-Naml. In it, an ant calls to the others to get out of the way of Solomon's army, and Solomon smiles at her words.
screen: `THE SLUGGARD ON HIS HINGES.` · `NO GUIDE, OVERSEER, OR RULER.` · `SUMMER WORK FOR WINTER BREAD.` · `LITTLE, BUT EXCEEDING WISE.` · then, large: `GO TO THE ANT.`

segments.voice: If you can, find something small at work nearby. Ants on a path. A bird carrying a twig. A bee at a flower. Even rain filling a gutter, or the second hand of a clock. If nothing's in sight, bring one to mind. Watch it without hurrying it. Notice that it doesn't wait for permission. Notice the small motion, repeated, steady. Let your breath settle to its pace. Then bring to mind one small piece of your own work that you could start now, before the season for it passes. If you pray, you can hold it in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Go to the ant. From Proverbs: the small creature that works with no overseer and gathers in summer for later. Today's word.
Your line: go to the ant. Today, start one task nobody is making you do, early, before it turns urgent. Day eight hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Some Jewish and Christian teachers use Proverbs 6:6 to teach diligence, sometimes alongside the lazy man of Proverbs 26, and the Qur'an names a surah for the ant.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scold for lazy people.
what it means: the ant works from inside, at the right time, with nobody watching.
what a scholar hears: Proverbs laughs at the slothful turning on his bed like a door on its hinges, and later calls the ants little upon the earth but exceeding wise.
